title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident describes a deliberate attempt to manipulate the training data or retrieval behavior of AI chatbots by seeding the web with fabricated authoritative sources. A website was constructed to resemble a legitimate American think tank, and a large volume of text formatted as academic research was published in a short window. A commercial tool was used specifically to optimize that content for AI citation. The failure mode is not one of the AI systems themselves behaving incorrectly in a conventional sense, but of those systems being exploited at the input layer, before any query is asked, by adversarially crafted content designed to look like the kind of material they are built to trust and repeat.

The vulnerability sits in how AI systems assign credibility to text. Chatbots trained on or retrieving from web sources have no reliable mechanism to verify whether a think tank is genuine, whether research was peer-reviewed, or whether a site was built in eight days for influence purposes. A human researcher encountering the Hanover Institute might check its provenance, funding history, or staff. AI systems operating at scale cannot routinely perform those checks, and the operation was explicitly designed to exploit that gap.

What is not established is whether any specific AI system was measurably caused to adopt or amplify the content's claims, and the reporting is based on a single outlet's account rather than an independent investigation or legal finding.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
Israeli government officials and contractors created a fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute to produce propaganda content designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. Between August 6 and 14, the site published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words, framing pro-Israel arguments on controversial topics like genocide allegations and Palestinian displacement. The reports were presented as academic research but persistently minimized criticism of Israel by claiming no court had ruled on genocide or apartheid claims. A commercial platform called Res was used to optimize the content so AI systems would cite it.

The operation is part of a larger campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government, routed through the advertising company Havas Media and contractors including former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale's Clock Tower X. Israeli officials have expressed frustration that public diplomacy spending has failed to improve Israel's standing in American public opinion, which has declined significantly since 2022. Researchers warn that using AI systems to spread narratives makes fact-checking difficult, as chatbots may repeat claims without citing sources or acknowledging the material's origin.
